Listen to this article Share President Bola Tinubu has asked the Senate to consider a bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide in Nigeria and provide support for people who attempt to take their own lives. Advertisement Advertisement The proposed Mental Health Bill 2026 was transmitted to the Senate in a letter read by Senate President Godswill Akpabio during plenary on Tuesday. In the letter, Tinubu urged the lawmakers to consider the proposed legislation, which seeks to change the country’s approach to attempted suicide by removing the criminal penalties associated with the act. The President also called for measures to provide support to anyone who attempts suicide in Nigeria. “While appreciating the Senate, I look forward to your usual expeditious consideration on this submission,” Tinubu said in the letter. The proposed legislation comes amid renewed conversations about the treatment of people who attempt suicide and whether criminal sanctions are an appropriate response to what is widely regarded as a public health and mental health concern. Advertisement Reacting to the President’s communication, Akpabio welcomed the proposed amendment, while revisiting the controversy surrounding his earlier comments on the criminalisation of attempted suicide. The Senate President had previously suggested that people who attempt suicide should ensure they succeed, otherwise they risk going to prison. Advertisement Clarifying his position on Tuesday, Akpabio said his earlier remarks were not directed at people experiencing mental health challenges, arguing that such individuals might not have the mental capacity to understand their actions. He said, “With this being now, I should make a distinction. My submission that if you are trying to commit suicide, you better make sure you succeed, otherwise we will send you to jail. Advertisement Advertisement “I did not include people who are mentally disturbed. I said so, I made that decision that I did not include people who are mentally disturbed, because they don’t have the mental balance to know what they are doing. “So I want to thank the President for decriminalising this, because to make it a criminal offence for people who are mentally disturbed would be to be insensitive.” Akpabio said the amendment was important, adding that people experiencing mental health challenges required support rather than criminal punishment. He said, “We are going to decriminalise all attempted suicides that have to do with people who are mentally disturbed. “I actually made that distinction, but when the social media carried it, they did not put the distinction. I said mentally sound people, I did not say people who are mentally disturbed. “Nevertheless, this is a good deal. People who are mentally disturbed require our support, and I know we will work on this.” The Senate President subsequently referred the proposed legislation to the Senate Committee on Rules and Business for further legislative action. The development follows an earlier motion sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who called on the Senate to decriminalise attempted suicide. The committee is expected to consider the proposed amendment and report back to the Senate as soon as practicable. The proposed legislation, if passed, would mark a significant shift in Nigeria’s response to attempted suicide, moving away from criminal punishment towards a framework that recognises the need for support and intervention.
